title: The Murle and the Pibor Region
subtitle: The rivers, settlements, livelihoods, history and political importance of Pibor within the wider Murle homeland
author: Murle Connect

body.heading: Pibor in the Murle Homeland
paragraphs: Pibor is one of the most important regions in the history and present life of the Murle people. It is both a geographical homeland and, in more recent history, an important administrative and political centre. However, Pibor should not be understood as another name for all Murle people or all Murle territory. The wider Murle homeland extends across the lowland plains and river systems around Pibor and toward the Boma highlands.

Murle sources commonly describe the people in two broad ecological groups: the larger lowland agro-pastoral population living across the plains associated with the Pibor, Veveno, Lotilla and Kengen rivers, and the agricultural population living in the Boma highlands. These differences are mainly connected to landscape, water, agriculture, livestock and seasonal movement rather than to separate ethnic identities.
For the Murle, therefore, Pibor is best understood as one major part of a larger homeland linking the lowlands and highlands.

body.heading: The Pibor River and the Rivers of the Lowlands
paragraphs: The rivers are central to understanding Murle life in the Pibor region. The Pibor, Veveno, Lotilla and Kengen rivers and their surrounding wetlands shape settlement, agriculture, livestock movement and access to water.

The Pibor River is particularly important because it runs through the centre of the lowland region and connects different parts of the landscape. The Veveno, Lotilla and Kengen systems are also closely associated with Murle settlement and seasonal livelihood patterns.

These rivers are not simply physical features on a map. They provide water during difficult seasons, support vegetation and agriculture, create grazing areas, and influence where people establish permanent settlements and temporary cattle camps.
The river valleys have historically attracted significant populations because access to water is essential in a landscape where rainfall and pasture vary considerably between seasons.

body.heading: The Lowland Murle and Lotilla Plains
paragraphs: The lowland Murle are sometimes described as Lotilla Murle or Lotillanya, a name connected with the Lotilla River and the plains where many lowland Murle live.

Their economy has traditionally combined cattle keeping with cultivation and other activities suited to the riverine and semi-arid environment. Cattle are important economically, socially and culturally, while agriculture provides food crops in places where soil, rainfall and water conditions permit.

Lowland life requires movement. During different parts of the year, families and cattle may use different parts of the landscape depending on water, pasture, crops and security. Temporary cattle camps are therefore an important feature of the traditional economy.

This seasonal movement should not be confused with the idea that the Murle have no permanent homeland. Movement takes place within a known cultural landscape whose rivers, grazing areas, hills, settlements and cattle camps are connected through generations of knowledge.

body.heading: Water, Cattle and Seasonal Movement
paragraphs: Cattle movement in the Pibor region follows the changing availability of pasture and water. Wetlands and river corridors can become particularly important during dry periods, while other areas become more suitable during the rainy season.

Research on the Pibor region has documented seasonal cattle movement toward areas such as the Jom Swamps near the Ethiopian border and cattle camps along the Kengen River. Such movements demonstrate how Murle pastoral life is adapted to the ecological cycles of the region.

The movement of cattle also connects communities that may live far apart during parts of the year. Families, age-sets and cattle camps can therefore create networks extending across much of the lowland homeland.

Historically, cattle have also been connected to marriage, wealth, social relationships and prestige. For this reason, cattle cannot be understood only as an economic resource. They form part of the social structure of Murle society.

body.heading: Agriculture in the Pibor Region
paragraphs: Although the Murle are often described from outside as pastoralists, agriculture has always been an important part of life, particularly where river systems, seasonal rainfall and fertile soils allow cultivation.

The ecological contrast between the lowlands and Boma creates different agricultural possibilities. The Boma highlands have more favourable conditions for intensive cultivation in many locations, while lowland agriculture is closely connected to seasonal rainfall and river environments.

Crops and livestock therefore complement one another. Farming provides food while livestock provides food, wealth and social resources. The balance between these activities has changed over time according to population movements, rainfall, conflict, disease and access to land and water.
The Pibor landscape should therefore be understood as an agro-pastoral environment rather than as a purely pastoral one.

body.heading: Pibor Town and Pibor Post
paragraphs: The importance of Pibor as an administrative centre has roots in the colonial period. The British established Pibor Post in 1912 after military campaigns that brought the Murle more firmly under colonial authority.

The creation of the post did not immediately transform the entire Murle homeland into a closely administered territory. Colonial administration remained limited for many years, particularly in remote areas. The Boma highlands and other parts of the region could remain difficult for government officials to reach.

Over time, however, Pibor Post developed into an important administrative centre. The town that grew around the post became increasingly significant for government administration, trade, humanitarian activity and communication.
This created an important distinction between Pibor as an old geographical and cultural region and Pibor town as a modern administrative and urban centre. The two should not be treated as identical.

body.heading: Gumuruk, Likuangole and Other Murle Centres
paragraphs: The wider Pibor region contains many settlements and rural communities beyond Pibor town. Gumuruk and Likuangole are among the places that have become important in modern Murle history.

These places are connected through roads, rivers, livestock routes, family relationships, age-set networks and administrative structures. Their importance has also changed according to war, displacement, government administration and the availability of services.

Gumuruk, in particular, has been an important centre in the western and northwestern parts of the wider Murle area. Likuangole has likewise played an important role in the eastern and southern parts of the lowland region.

The history of the Murle cannot therefore be reduced to the history of Pibor town. The villages, cattle camps and rural areas surrounding the main centres are equally important to understanding how Murle society has survived and developed.

body.heading: Kong Kong and the Wider Rural Landscape
paragraphs: The rural landscape around Pibor contains many smaller communities, cattle camps and seasonal settlement areas that may not appear prominently on modern maps.
Kong Kong, for example, is associated with Murle rural life and has been documented as a location where Murle youth and age-set communities have lived and identified themselves.

Such places demonstrate an important characteristic of Murle geography: the homeland is not made up only of towns and administrative headquarters. Much of its history has been lived in villages, cattle camps, river valleys, hills and seasonal grazing areas.

Understanding this rural geography is essential because administrative maps often simplify landscapes that local people understand through much more detailed systems of ancestry, livestock routes, water sources, cultivation areas and community relationships.

body.heading: The Relationship Between Pibor and Boma
paragraphs: Pibor and Boma represent two major ecological zones within the wider Murle homeland. Pibor is associated primarily with the lowland plains and river systems, while Boma is associated with the highlands and agricultural communities.

The difference between these environments produced different livelihood patterns. Lowland Murle historically depended heavily on livestock and seasonal movement, while highland Murle developed stronger agricultural systems suited to the Boma Plateau.

These differences sometimes produced different political experiences and historical relationships with neighbouring communities. They should not, however, be interpreted as evidence that the two populations are separate peoples.
Murle cultural institutions cross the ecological divide. Language, clans, age-sets, ancestral traditions and shared historical memory connect communities from Boma to Pibor.

The statement often expressed in Murle historical accounts that people from Boma and Pibor share the same language, clans and identity reflects this deeper connection: the highlands and lowlands form different environments within a wider Murle homeland.

body.heading: Pibor as a Borderland
paragraphs: The Pibor region lies within a wider borderland linking South Sudan and Ethiopia. The landscape has historically brought Murle into contact with several neighbouring peoples, including Dinka, Nuer, Anyuak, Jie and Kachipo communities.
These relationships have included trade, intermarriage, movement, cooperation, competition over resources and periods of serious conflict. The exact nature of each relationship has changed over time.
The rivers and wetlands have made the region both a meeting place and a contested space. During periods of drought or insecurity, access to pasture and water can become especially important.

The border with Ethiopia also means that the Pibor region cannot be understood only within the modern boundaries of South Sudan. Movement, trade, migration and historical connections have long crossed the frontier.

body.heading: Colonial Administration and the Pibor Region
paragraphs: British colonial administration changed the political geography of the Pibor region. The Pibor Post established in 1912 became a centre from which the colonial government attempted to administer the surrounding territory.

At first, colonial control was limited and relied heavily on patrols, military expeditions and indirect administration. Over time, the government introduced courts, chiefs appointed or recognized by the administration, taxation and other institutions of colonial rule.

The colonial government also attempted to restrict cattle raiding and regulate relations between communities. These policies affected traditional institutions and the responsibilities that had previously been associated with age-sets and customary authorities.

The colonial period therefore changed Pibor without eliminating Murle institutions. Traditional authority, clan relationships, age-sets and local customs continued alongside new administrative structures.

body.heading: Pibor After Sudanese Independence
paragraphs: After Sudan became independent in 1956, Pibor remained a remote region within southern Sudan. Government authority continued to be limited in many rural areas, while the region experienced the wider political instability that affected southern Sudan.
The First Sudanese Civil War, the Anyanya period, the Second Sudanese Civil War and the political transition surrounding the Comprehensive Peace Agreement all affected the Pibor region.

War increased population movement, disrupted agriculture and education, changed cattle patterns and created new forms of military organization. At the same time, Pibor became increasingly important in the political demands of communities seeking greater local representation.
The region's geographical isolation meant that the lack of roads, schools, hospitals and government services remained a major issue even after the creation of South Sudan.

body.heading: Pibor and the Birth of the Greater Pibor Administrative Area
paragraphs: The political importance of Pibor increased sharply after South Sudan became independent in 2011. Grievances over political representation, security, disarmament and relations with the state contributed to the rebellion associated with David Yau Yau and the Cobra Faction.

A peace agreement between the South Sudanese government and the Cobra Faction was signed in May 2014. The agreement provided for the creation of the Greater Pibor Administrative Area, or GPAA, covering the former Pibor and Pochalla counties within Jonglei State.

The new administrative arrangement was significant because it gave the area a special administrative status and placed it under a chief administrator whose status was intended to be equivalent to that of a state governor.

The creation of the GPAA was therefore not simply an administrative boundary change. It was also the result of a political struggle over representation, local authority, security and the relationship between the Pibor region and the central government.

body.heading: From GPAA to Boma State and Back to a Pibor Administrative Area
paragraphs: The administrative history of the region continued to change after 2014. In 2015, the former GPAA arrangement was replaced during the creation of new states, including Boma State.
Boma was consequently separated administratively from the earlier GPAA arrangement even though the social and cultural connections between Boma and the Pibor lowlands remained.

In February 2020, President Salva Kiir announced a return from 32 states to the earlier system of 10 states and three administrative areas. Pibor was again constituted as a special administrative area.

These repeated administrative changes demonstrate an important point for Murle history: political boundaries have changed several times within a relatively short period, while cultural relationships between communities, clans, rivers and landscapes are much older.
For historical writing, it is therefore important not to project today's administrative boundaries backward onto earlier periods.

body.heading: Pibor and Murle Political Identity
paragraphs: Pibor became one of the main centres through which Murle political identity was expressed during the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Government administration, military campaigns, elections, rebellions and peace negotiations repeatedly focused attention on the region.

The political importance of Pibor does not mean that all Murle communities have always shared identical political views. Murle society has historically been decentralized, and different areas, age-sets, chiefs, elders and political leaders have sometimes followed different paths.
The region's politics must therefore be understood through both local diversity and wider Murle identity.

Pibor has also become a place where the Murle encounter the wider South Sudanese state. Government offices, security forces, humanitarian organizations, schools, health facilities and political institutions are concentrated there more than in many rural areas.

body.heading: Pibor and the Challenges of Modern Development
paragraphs: The Pibor region has faced severe challenges in developing roads, schools, health services, markets and reliable communications. Geographic isolation, seasonal flooding, conflict and limited infrastructure have all affected development.
The result is that many communities remain strongly dependent on livestock, cultivation and local natural resources while also relying on humanitarian assistance during periods of crisis.

Development in Pibor cannot be separated from the environment. Roads must cross wetlands and rivers, communities depend on seasonal water sources, and cattle routes need to coexist with agricultural land and permanent settlements.
Long-term development therefore requires an understanding of the region's own ecological and cultural systems rather than treating Pibor as an ordinary urban district.

body.heading: Pibor in Murle Memory
paragraphs: For many Murle, Pibor is more than a place on a political map. It is connected to family histories, cattle camps, rivers, settlements, migrations and memories of conflict and survival.

Older generations remember a Pibor landscape before many modern roads, government offices and administrative boundaries existed. Younger generations experience the same homeland through schools, mobile phones, towns, government institutions and migration between South Sudan and other countries.
The landscape remains a living archive. A river can identify a region, a hill can preserve an ancestral memory, and a cattle camp can connect generations of families.

This is why Murle history cannot be written only through government records. Administrative documents explain how states attempted to govern Pibor, while oral histories explain how Murle communities understood and inhabited the land.

body.heading: Pibor Is Part of a Larger Murle Homeland
paragraphs: The history of Pibor must finally be placed within the larger history of the Murle people. Pibor is one of the central regions of Murle life, but it is not the whole of Murle country.

The lowland plains, Boma highlands, river systems, villages and cattle camps form a connected cultural landscape. People may move between these environments for farming, livestock, marriage, education, trade, security or family reasons.
Modern administrative boundaries have repeatedly divided and reorganized this landscape, but they have not erased the older relationships between Murle communities.
From Boma to Pibor, from the highlands to the river plains, Murle identity has been maintained through language, ancestry, clans, age-sets, customs and shared memory.
Pibor is therefore best understood not as a replacement for the wider Murle homeland, but as one of its most important geographical, historical and political centres.

historicalNote: Pibor has both an older geographical meaning within the Murle homeland and a newer administrative meaning. The lowland Murle homeland extends across the plains associated with the Pibor, Veveno, Lotilla and Kengen rivers, while the wider Murle homeland also includes the Boma highlands. Pibor Post was established by the British in 1912, but colonial administration remained limited in many parts of the region for decades. The Greater Pibor Administrative Area was created through the May 2014 peace agreement between the South Sudanese government and the Cobra Faction. The administrative arrangement changed again with the creation of Boma State in 2015 and the re-establishment of Pibor as a special administrative area in 2020. These modern administrative boundaries should not be projected backward onto older Murle history.
